title: Ukraine Airdrops Food by Drone to Starving Occupied City
summary:
Ukrainian officials say they have carried out a large-scale food airdrop into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city on the brink of starvation. Drones dropped four tonnes of food — boxes of supplies and cooking oil — at 100 different locations across the community on Saturday, according to regional authorities. The operation involved several Ukrainian military units and was carried out in waves. Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told CBC News that drone video confirmed some residents received the food. He said the Ukrainian military has carried out several other aid drops since April, but they were on a much smaller scale.

Oleshky lies just three kilometres south of the Dnipro River, which forms the front line between Ukrainian forces controlling Kherson and Russian forces occupying communities on the left bank. Before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, about 20,000 people lived there. Ukrainian officials estimate only about 6,000 remain today, including roughly 200 children.

"This will give people the opportunity to live there for up to a month," Tolokonnikov said. But he warned the relief could be short-lived, and said Russian troops forcibly seized supplies from civilians in some cases.

Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha told the UN General Assembly that residents are under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, which he said are refusing to allow humanitarian aid in. He called on the international community to pressure Russia to open an evacuation corridor. Russia has acknowledged critical shortages of food and medicine in the city but says its forces are working to address the problems.

Oleshky has no functioning stores, and the nearest supplies are about 20 kilometres away, in the rural community of Radensk. A woman whose 70-year-old mother-in-law left the city after walking six hours told CBC News that people have been constantly searching for food, sometimes obtaining only two potatoes and two pieces of garlic. She said people have been bartering with neighbours, trading things like vegetables for eggs. Others, officials say, have resorted to foraging for weeds. Tetiana Hasanenko, the Ukrainian head of the Oleshky military administration working in exile, shared a message from a resident describing how people exchange information about how to cook "grass and weeds that grow in the gardens." Reports from inside the city are difficult to verify independently, as residents fear reprisals for speaking publicly.
why_it_matters: The siege of Oleshky shows how modern wars hurt civilians most: blockades and destroyed infrastructure can produce starvation without a single battle, and the international rules meant to prevent that only work if other countries are willing to enforce them.

background_read: Oleshky sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, a major river that has served as the front line in southern Ukraine since Ukrainian forces retook the city of Kherson in November 2022. Ukrainian troops hold the right bank; Russian forces occupy the left bank, including Oleshky.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Oleshky was occupied within the first weeks of the war. In June 2023 the Kakhovka Dam upstream was destroyed, sending floodwater through towns on the left bank, including Oleshky — an event that made an already difficult humanitarian situation far worse.

Under international humanitarian law — the rules of war set out in treaties such as the Geneva Conventions — civilians must be allowed access to food, water and medical care, and starving a population as a method of war is prohibited. Aid agencies rely on agreed corridors to move supplies; without them, deliveries have to be improvised, often by drone.

The UN General Assembly, where Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke, is the yearly gathering of all UN member states in New York, where leaders give speeches aimed at building international pressure and hold meetings on the sidelines.
Airdrops are rare and risky: food can land in the wrong place, be damaged, or be seized before it reaches people, and they cannot replace a working supply route.

perspectives.description: Regional authorities present the drone drops as proof that Ukraine has not abandoned residents under occupation, and Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha uses the 'full blockade' charge to press the international community for an evacuation corridor. They argue the operation restores a basic obligation that Russia is violating.

Russia acknowledges critical shortages of food and medicine but says its forces are working to fix them, denying that it is deliberately starving the city. From this angle, the Ukrainian airdrops are a publicity gesture that cannot substitute for a real aid route.

Analysts point to a repeating pattern in modern sieges: cutting supply lines is used as a weapon, and civilians become leverage. They also note that airdrops are expensive, unreliable, and can be seized — four tonnes covering roughly a month is a stopgap, not a solution, and independent verification inside occupied territory is nearly impossible.

The key question is access. If Russia refuses an evacuation corridor, the choice is between continued risky drone drops, negotiated pauses, or doing nothing. How the UN and donor countries respond will shape whether other besieged communities can expect help in the future.
